title: Child death review and serious incident learning
blurb: Follow a child's death through notification, joint agency response, the review meeting, CDOP and NCMD, and know how serious safeguarding incidents are reviewed.
question: A 7-month-old is brought into the emergency department after being found unresponsive at home and cannot be resuscitated. There is no obvious cause. Which child death review processes now begin, and what is the nurse's part?

teach.body: In England every death of a child (under 18) is reviewed, whatever the cause. The aim is to learn what happened and why, identify modifiable factors and prevent future deaths, while supporting the family. Responsibility sits with the child death review partners: the local authority and the integrated care board (ICB) for the area. Plain English: no child's death is filed away without someone asking what could be learned.
teach.cite: Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026, Chapter 6; Children Act 2004 s16M-16Q

steps.label: A child dies
steps.sub: Notify CDOP via the child death notification form

steps.label: Immediate decisions
steps.sub: Notifications; joint agency response if criteria met

steps.label: Investigation
steps.sub: Information gathering; coroner, police if needed

steps.label: NCMD
steps.sub: National analysis of all deaths reviewed

teach.caption: CDOP = Child Death Overview Panel. NCMD = National Child Mortality Database.

teach.h: When a joint agency response is needed
head: The death...
Example
rows: Is or could be due to external causes
Is sudden with no apparent cause
Occurs in custody or under the MHA
Young person detained in a secure unit
Raises suspicion it was not natural
Injuries that do not fit the history
Is a stillbirth with no professional present
teach.caption: Joint agency response follows the RCPCH 'Sudden unexpected death in infancy and childhood' multi-agency guidelines (2016).

teach.h: Unexpected death at home: ED, not mortuary
teach.body: If a child dies unexpectedly at home or in the community, the child should normally be taken to a hospital emergency department rather than a mortuary, unless police decide the body must stay for forensic examination. Staff should offer every bereaved family the guide 'When a child dies: a guide for parents and carers' and consider support for staff involved too.

rows.label: Who
values: Professionals directly involved in life or after death
Independent professionals with no responsibility for the child

rows.label: Focus
values: All matters about this child's death

rows.label: Output
values: Draft analysis form sent to CDOP
Data to NCMD; actions and annual report

teach.body: Modifiable factors are factors that may have contributed to the child's death and that might, through a locally or nationally achievable intervention, be changed to reduce the risk of future deaths. Example: a CDOP finds several infant deaths involving co-sleeping after parental alcohol use and recommends a local safer sleep campaign.

items.label: Serious incident notification to the Panel
Rapid review submitted to the Panel
Local Child Safeguarding Practice Review, if decided

teach.caption: s16C Children Act 2004: the local authority notifies the Child Safeguarding Practice Review Panel when abuse or neglect is known or suspected and a child dies or is seriously harmed.

teach.h: Worked scenario: baby Oscar in ED
items: Oscar, 7 months, is brought to ED by ambulance after being found unresponsive in his cot. Resuscitation fails. There is no obvious cause.
This is a sudden unexpected death in infancy, so a joint agency response is triggered (health and police together).
Nurse Tom stays with the parents, offers the 'When a child dies' guide, records accurately what was said and done, and preserves items as directed.
The death is notified to the CDOP administrator; Tom later contributes to the child death review meeting.

teach.text: Do not confuse the two learning routes. EVERY child death goes through child death review (CDR partners, CDOP, NCMD). Only deaths or serious harm where abuse or neglect is known or suspected also trigger a serious incident notification, rapid review and possibly an LCSPR.

items: Child death review partners: local authority + ICB. Reviews via CDOP; national analysis by NCMD.
Joint agency response: external cause, sudden unexplained, custody or MHA, suspicious, or unattended stillbirth.
Unexplained death at home: child normally taken to ED, not a mortuary.
Review meeting = people who knew the child; CDOP = independent final scrutiny.
Abuse or neglect suspected: notify the Panel within 5 working days; rapid review within 15 working days.

summary: You can now describe the child death review pathway from notification to CDOP and NCMD, recognise when a joint agency response is needed, and support the family. You can also distinguish routine child death review from the serious incident notification and rapid review that follow suspected abuse or neglect.

A.q: A student nurse asks which bodies in England are responsible for making sure every child death in their area is reviewed. What is the correct answer?
options: The coroner and the police
The NHS trust and the GP
The local authority and the ICB
The three safeguarding partners
A.why: Child death review partners are the local authority and any ICB for the local area (Children Act 2004 as amended).

whyNot.0: The coroner investigates certain deaths and the police may investigate, but neither is a child death review partner.
whyNot.1: Trusts and GPs contribute information but do not hold the statutory responsibility.
whyNot.3: The three safeguarding partners (LA, ICB, police) lead safeguarding arrangements; child death review partners are LA and ICB.

A.q: Which child's death requires a joint agency response?
options: A 5-month-old found dead in a cot with no obvious cause
A 10-year-old with leukaemia dying in a hospice as planned
A 3-day-old preterm baby dying on the neonatal unit from expected complications
A 15-year-old with cystic fibrosis dying on a respiratory ward
A.why: A sudden death with no immediately apparent cause, including sudden unexpected death in infancy, requires a joint agency response.

whyNot.1: An expected death from a known life-limiting condition does not meet the criteria; it still goes through child death review.
whyNot.2: An expected neonatal death from known complications is reviewed but does not need a joint agency response.
whyNot.3: This is an expected death from a known condition; it is reviewed through the usual process.

A.q: Where is information from all child death reviews in England analysed nationally?
options: The Child Safeguarding Practice Review Panel
The Office for National Statistics
The Care Quality Commission
The National Child Mortality Database
A.why: Child death review partners must arrange for information from all deaths reviewed to be analysed by the NCMD.

whyNot.0: The Panel oversees serious safeguarding incidents, not all child deaths.
whyNot.1: The ONS publishes registration statistics but does not analyse child death reviews.
whyNot.2: The CQC regulates health and care providers; it does not hold the national child death review data.

B.q: Ruby, 3, dies unexpectedly at home. Paramedics find no signs of life and police do not require her to stay at the scene. Where should she normally be taken?
options: The local mortuary
A hospital emergency department
The nearest children's hospice
The coroner's office
B.why: WT 2026 says a child who dies unexpectedly at home or in the community should normally be taken to an emergency department rather than a mortuary.

whyNot.0: The guidance specifically says ED rather than a mortuary for an unexplained death.
whyNot.2: Hospices care for children with expected deaths; this death is unexplained and needs assessment.
whyNot.3: The coroner may investigate, but the child is not taken to a coroner's office.

B.q: Josh, 4, died from sepsis on a children's ward. A multi-agency meeting is held before the CDOP review. Who should attend this child death review meeting?
options: CDOP members with no previous contact with Josh
The ward consultant and registrar on duty
The coroner and the designated doctor
Professionals involved in Josh's care or the investigation
B.why: The child death review meeting is attended by professionals directly involved in the child's care in life or in the investigation after death, and is not limited to medical staff.

whyNot.0: Independent professionals with no responsibility for the child form the CDOP, which meets later.
whyNot.1: WT 2026 says the meeting should not be limited to medical staff; nurses and others who knew Josh also attend.
whyNot.2: The coroner does not routinely attend; the meeting brings together those who knew the child.

B.q: A CDOP is reviewing an infant death. What are 'modifiable factors'?
options: Factors that may have contributed and could be changed to prevent deaths
Factors that prove the parents caused the death
Errors by individual staff that need disciplinary action
Factors recorded on the medical certificate of cause of death
B.why: Modifiable factors may have contributed to the death and might be changed by achievable local or national interventions to reduce future deaths.

whyNot.1: Child death review is about learning, not proving fault; criminal matters are for the police.
whyNot.2: The process is not a disciplinary route; it looks for system learning.
whyNot.3: The certificate records cause of death; modifiable factors are wider contributing factors.

C.q: Mia, 2, dies in hospital from head injuries. Abuse is suspected. Which process must happen in addition to child death review, and within what time?
options: A rapid review submitted within 5 working days
A serious incident notification to the Panel within 15 working days
A serious incident notification to the Panel within 5 working days
A local practice review completed within 15 working days
C.why: Where abuse or neglect is known or suspected and a child dies, the local authority notifies the Child Safeguarding Practice Review Panel within 5 working days; a rapid review follows within 15 working days.

whyNot.0: The rapid review is due within 15 working days of notification, not 5.
whyNot.1: The notification is due within 5 working days; 15 working days is the rapid review.
whyNot.3: An LCSPR, if decided, should be completed within 6 months.

C.q: Baby Amelia, 4 months, has died unexpectedly in ED and a joint agency response has started. Her parents are distraught. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
options: Ask the parents to leave while the police assess
Stay with the parents and offer the 'When a child dies' guide
Explain that a post-mortem means the parents are suspected
Remove Amelia's clothing and wash her before they hold her
C.why: Supporting the family is central; WT 2026 says the 'When a child dies' guide should be offered to all bereaved families. Nurses work alongside police in a joint response.

whyNot.0: Parents should be supported and kept informed, not sent away, unless police direct otherwise for a specific reason.
whyNot.2: Post-mortems are routine in unexplained deaths; saying this implies blame and is inaccurate.
whyNot.3: In an unexplained death, items and the child's presentation may need preserving; follow the joint agency protocol.

C.q: A CDOP reviews three infant deaths in its area linked to unsafe sleeping. Which action best fulfils the purpose of child death review?
options: Refer each family to the police for investigation
Close the cases as natural deaths
Request disciplinary action against the health visitors
Recommend a local safer sleep intervention
C.why: CDR partners identify matters relevant to children's welfare or public health and must inform anyone who should take action; a prevention campaign targets a modifiable factor.

whyNot.0: Police referral is for suspected crime, which these reviews have not identified.
whyNot.1: Closing cases misses the purpose: learning to prevent future deaths.
whyNot.2: Child death review is not a disciplinary process.

reteach.title: Two different learning routes
reteach.question: Why does a child who dies of leukaemia in a hospice go through one process, while a child who dies after suspected abuse goes through two?

blocks.h: One route for all, one extra for abuse
blocks.body: Child death review is universal: every child death goes from notification to a review meeting, to CDOP and NCMD. When abuse or neglect is known or suspected and a child dies or is seriously harmed, the local authority also starts the serious incident route: notify the Panel, rapid review, then possibly a Local Child Safeguarding Practice Review.

children.label: Child death review: CDOP and NCMD

children.edge: Abuse or neglect known or suspected
children.label: ALSO serious incident notification (5 working days)

blocks.text: 5 working days = notification. 15 working days = rapid review. 6 months = LCSPR.

explain.body: The local authority and ICB are the child death review partners. They review all deaths of children normally resident in their area through a CDOP, covering a population large enough to review at least 60 deaths a year, and send data to the NCMD.

test.q: Which organisation is a safeguarding partner but NOT a child death review partner?
options: The police
The local authority
The integrated care board
The NHS trust
test.why: Safeguarding partners are LA, ICB and police; child death review partners are LA and ICB only.

whyNot.1: The LA is both a safeguarding partner and a CDR partner.
whyNot.3: An NHS trust is neither; it cooperates with both.

explain.body: Health and police respond together when a death is or could be from external causes, is sudden and unexplained, happens in custody or under the Mental Health Act, raises suspicion, or is a stillbirth with no professional present.

test.q: Which death meets the criteria for a joint agency response?
options: A 12-year-old dying of a brain tumour at home as planned
A 2-day-old dying from a known heart defect on NICU
A 9-year-old drowning in a swimming pool
A 16-year-old dying of an expected end-stage condition
test.why: Drowning is an external cause, so a joint agency response is required.

whyNot.0: An expected, planned death at home does not meet the criteria.
whyNot.1: An expected neonatal death from a known condition does not meet the criteria.
whyNot.3: This is an expected death; it is reviewed through standard child death review.

explain.body: The child death review meeting brings together everyone involved in the child's life and death, then sends a draft analysis form to CDOP. CDOP gives final, independent scrutiny by people with no responsibility for the child, identifying modifiable factors.

test.q: What makes the CDOP review different from the child death review meeting?
options: It is attended by the bereaved family
Its members had no responsibility for the child
It decides whether a crime was committed
It happens before any investigation starts
test.why: CDOP is intended as the final, independent scrutiny by professionals with no responsibility for the child in life.

whyNot.0: Families are supported and kept informed but are not CDOP members.
whyNot.2: Criminal decisions belong to police and the CPS.
whyNot.3: CDOP is the last stage, after investigation and the review meeting.

explain.body: Under s16C Children Act 2004, if abuse or neglect is known or suspected and a child dies or is seriously harmed, the local authority notifies the Panel within 5 working days. A rapid review follows within 15 working days, and an LCSPR, if decided, within 6 months.

test.q: Within what time must a rapid review be submitted to the Panel after a serious incident notification?
options: 5 working days
10 working days
45 working days
15 working days
test.why: WT 2026: rapid reviews are submitted to the Panel within 15 working days of notification.

whyNot.0: 5 working days is the deadline for the notification itself.
whyNot.1: 10 working days is when a core group meets after an initial conference.
whyNot.2: 45 working days is the maximum time for an assessment.
